subject: cheats: fix assume not precompile (#594)
body:
* cheats: fix assume not precompile

After the cancun hardfork, the point evaluation precompile was added
at `address(10)` which the `assumeNotPrecompile` implementation
did not take into account. Pectra is scheduled to include BLS
precompiles and likely more precompiles will be introduced in
other future hardforks. We might as well reserve the least significant
byte for Ethereum precompiles, as the address space is large and there
is no need to make calls from these addresses, and in return code
will not break on new EVM specs.

This was causing test failures in the Optimism test suite when
we updated the EVM version to cancun.

* cheats: update typo

Use the address range of precomiples that testnets use,
see https://github.com/eth-clients/holesky/blob/main/metadata/genesis.json
rationale: The change expands the address range excluded by assumeNotPrecompile to include new precompile addresses (0x10‑0xff). This corrects test behavior after the Cancun hardfork but does not affect production security, as the code is a testing cheat helper.

subject: feat: add ERC7540 and ERC7575 interfaces (#644)
body:
This adds the interfaces for the 2 finalized extensions to ERC4626,
[ERC7540](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7540) and
[ERC7575](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7575). See
https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/standards/tokens/erc-4626/#introduction
for details on these extensions.

Adding these would be helpful for repositories that rely on the
interfaces in `forge-std`.

ERC7540 interfaces are split by async deposit, async redeem, and fully
async vaults, per the ERC specification. This also ensures the ERC-165
ID matches for each vault type.

The ERC7575 interface specifies all ERC4626 methods, rather than
extending `IERC4626.sol`, because:
1. ERC20 methods need to be excluded for ERC7575.
2. This ensures `IERC7575.interfaceId` is the expected ID as specified
in https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7575#erc-165-support, since
`.interfaceID` does not account for inherited interfaces.
rationale: The commit only introduces new interface files (IERC7540.sol and IERC7575.sol) without modifying existing logic. It adds no functional changes, bug corrections, or security-related checks, so it is a feature addition rather than a bug or security fix.

subject: perf(StdAssertions): avoid vm call for trivial conditions (#693)
body:
Avoid calling vm when the condition is trivial to check inline. This is
a minor performance improvement as a couple of opcodes execute a lot
faster than a full cheatcode pipeline (external call, EVM call
bookkeeping, abi encoding/decoding, ...) that eventually does nothing.

For example, [Uniswap's v4-core](https://github.com/Uniswap/v4-core/)
spends ~28% of the entire `forge test` CPU time in a couple of trivial
`assert` functions (uint256, bytes32, true, false), ~13% for `forge
coverage`. This is without accounting for the actual CALL/abi coding
etc.

These numbers are skewed due to profiling overhead, however making this
change does have ~5% overall test performance improvement, for no
compilation time change.
rationale: The change only adds trivial condition checks before calling vm.assert* functions to avoid unnecessary VM calls, which is a performance optimization. It does not correct incorrect behavior nor introduce or fix a security issue.

subject: feat(console): add console.table (#849)
body:
Resolves #91

- Depends on https://github.com/foundry-rs/foundry/pull/14338

Two of the most common use-cases for tables are easily logging arrays
and comparing multiple labelled values, which often leads the user to
manually line up the values like so:

```solidity
console.log("alice  ", 0x328809Bc894f92807417D2dAD6b7C998c1aFdac6);
console.log("bob    ", 0x1D96F2f6BeF1202E4Ce1Ff6Dad0c2CB002861d3e);
console.log("charlie", 0xea475d60c118d7058beF4bDd9c32bA51139a74e0);
```

Both of those use-cases can be solved with a table with a single column
of values. For this reason and because it would double the variants,
I've opted to not support tables with multiple value columns, though it
can be added in the future.

This adds 12 variants for `console.table`:
- 6 single-array (auto-indexed, array of values)
- 6 keyed (`string[]` indexes, array of values)

Value types supported: `uint256`, `int256`, `address`, `bytes32`,
`string`, `bool`.

Some notes:
- I've added this to `console` and not `console2` since it's just adding
new functionality and not introducing any breaking changes. For
`console2` to inherit from `console` and have its own new methods, I
would need to import each method from `console` and define new ones in
`console2` since libraries don't support inheritance, which would be a
lot of maintenance, and also would involve the question of whether to
use the same `CONSOLE_ADDRESS`
- I've chosen the box characters `┌`, `─`, `┼`, `│`, etc. to more
closely match Node.js's `console.table` output and because it's more
aesthetically pleasing, but if preferred, a simpler option is to use the
ASCII version with just `-`, `+`, `|`

Usage example:

```solidity
string[] memory idxs = new string[](3);
idxs[0] = "alice";
idxs[1] = "bob";
idxs[2] = "charlie";
address[] memory addrs = new address[](3);
bytes32[] memory hashes = new bytes32[](3);
for (uint256 i = 0; i < idxs.length; i++) {
    addrs[i] = makeAddr(idxs[i]);
    hashes[i] = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(idxs[i]));
}
console.table(addrs);
console.table(idxs, addrs);
console.table(idxs, hashes);
```

Output:

```txt
Logs:
  ┌─────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ (index) │ Values                                     │
  ├─────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 0       │ 0x328809Bc894f92807417D2dAD6b7C998c1aFdac6 │
  │ 1       │ 0x1D96F2f6BeF1202E4Ce1Ff6Dad0c2CB002861d3e │
  │ 2       │ 0xea475d60c118d7058beF4bDd9c32bA51139a74e0 │
  └─────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ (index) │ Values                                     │
  ├─────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ alice   │ 0x328809Bc894f92807417D2dAD6b7C998c1aFdac6 │
  │ bob     │ 0x1D96F2f6BeF1202E4Ce1Ff6Dad0c2CB002861d3e │
  │ charlie │ 0xea475d60c118d7058beF4bDd9c32bA51139a74e0 │
  └─────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ (index) │ Values                                                             │
  ├─────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ alice   │ 0x9c0257114eb9399a2985f8e75dad7600c5d89fe3824ffa99ec1c3eb8bf3b0501 │
  │ bob     │ 0x38e47a7b719dce63662aeaf43440326f551b8a7ee198cee35cb5d517f2d296a2 │
  │ charlie │ 0x87a213ce1ee769e28decedefb98f6fe48890a74ba84957ebf877fb591e37e0de │
```

subject: fix(config): let config-only chains load without an RPC endpoint (#903)
body:
The `StdConfig` constructor resolves an RPC endpoint for every chain
section, and fails the whole load when neither `endpoint_url` nor
`[rpc_endpoints]` supplies one:

```solidity
try vm.parseTomlString(content, string.concat("$.", chain_key, ".endpoint_url")) returns (string memory url) {
    _rpcOf[chainId] = vm.resolveEnv(url);
} catch {
    _rpcOf[chainId] = vm.resolveEnv(vm.rpcUrl(chain_key));
}
```

`_rpcOf` is only read by `getRpcUrl`, and `getRpcUrl` is only called by
`_loadConfigAndForks` when it creates forks. So a chain section that
exists purely to carry config values is rejected for lacking something
nothing on that path would ever read:

```toml
[anvil]
endpoint_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8545"

[optimism.uint]
some_number = 7
```

```
[FAIL: invalid rpc url: optimism]
```

This defers the resolution. Loading such a chain now succeeds and its
values stay readable. Asking for the endpoint reverts with
`MissingRpcEndpoint(chainId)`.

## Behaviour change worth flagging

`getRpcUrl` previously returned an empty string for a chain with no
endpoint, and now reverts. That is deliberate, since a caller asking for
an endpoint that does not exist is better off knowing than receiving
`""`, and it gives `_loadConfigAndForks` a failure that names the chain
rather than the previous `invalid rpc url`. Nothing changes for a chain
that has an endpoint configured. Happy to return the empty string
instead if you would rather keep it non-reverting.

## Tests

Two cases in `test/Config.t.sol`, following the temp-fixture pattern
already used by the `testRevert_` tests:

- `test_loadConfigWithoutRpcEndpoint` loads a config with one
endpoint-less chain, asserts both chains load, that the config values
are readable, and that a configured endpoint still resolves.
- `testRevert_MissingRpcEndpoint` asserts the endpoint lookup reverts
for that chain.

```
forge test                  208 passed, 0 failed
forge fmt --check           clean
forge build --deny warnings clean
```

Negative control: reverting only the constructor change, leaving the new
error declared so it still compiles, makes both new tests fail with
`invalid rpc url: optimism` while the other nine in the file are
unaffected.

## Context

Reported as foundry-rs/foundry#13119. The premise there does not
reproduce on current `master`: the config in that issue loads fine,
empty chain sections are already skipped at `StdConfig.sol:100`, and a
missing type sub-section is already tolerated by the surrounding `try
... catch {}`. This is the adjacent gap that is real.
rationale: The change fixes a regression where StdConfig would reject config-only chains lacking an RPC endpoint, allowing such chains to load correctly. This is a functional bug fix, not a security vulnerability.

subject: fix(StdStorage): handle signed fields narrower than 256 bits (#904)
body:
A getter whose return type is a signed integer narrower than 256 bits
ABI-encodes its value **sign-extended**, while storage holds only the
field's own bits. `int64(-5)` comes back from the call as

```
0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffb
```

but sits in the slot as `0x…fffffffffffffffb`. `find` compares the two
directly:

```solidity
uint256 curVal = (uint256(prev) & getMaskByOffsets(offsetLeft, offsetRight)) >> offsetRight;
if (!shortBytesFound && uint256(callData.result) != curVal) continue;
```

so they never match and the loop walks past the slot that actually holds
the value:

```
stdStorage find(StdStorage): Slot(s) not found.
```

## Scope

Any negative value in an `int8`…`int248` field, whether it shares a slot
or sits in one alone, and with or without `enable_packed_slots`.

- Full-width `int256` is unaffected — there is nothing to extend. The
existing `test_StorageReadInt` (`type(int256).min`) keeps passing.
- Unsigned fields are unaffected — their high bits are already zero.

## Changes

Three changes, one cause:

1. **`find`** compares the call result truncated to the field's width.
For a full-width field the mask is all ones, so this is a no-op.
2. **`read_int`** sign-extends the extracted field back to `int256` from
the field's width. Without this, `find` succeeds but the value reads as
its zero-extension — `18446744073709551611` instead of `-5`.
3. **`checked_write`** narrows a sign-extended negative back to the
field before the fit check. Previously `checked_write_int(-42)` on a
packed field tripped the packed-slot bound with a misleading message
about not fitting a value *"greater than 18446744073709551616"*. The
getter still returns the sign-extended form, so the write verification
below is unchanged.

`read_int` no longer routes through `_read`, since it needs the field
width; `_read` is still used by `read_bytes32` / `read_address` /
`read_uint`, which must **not** sign-extend. `read_bool` delegates to
`read_int` and is unaffected (0 and 1 extend to themselves).

## Test plan

Four tests added next to the existing `test_StorageReadInt`, plus narrow
signed fields on `StorageTest` (`int64 tJ` packed with `uint64 tK`, and
`int8 tSolo` pushed into its own slot by a following `uint256`). All
state vars are appended, and nothing in the suite hardcodes a slot index
— every test discovers slots via `find()`.

Verified by reverting **only** `src/StdStorage.sol` and keeping the
tests:

| test | without the fix |
| --- | --- |
| `test_StorageReadIntPackedNegative` | `Slot(s) not found.` |
| `test_StorageReadIntSoloNegative` | `Slot(s) not found.` |
| `test_StorageWriteIntPackedNegative` | `Slot(s) not found.` |
| `test_StorageReadIntPackedPositiveSibling` | passes — regression
guard, green either way by design |

`forge test` is green: **210 passed, 0 failed** (206 before, plus these
4), including the whole existing StdStorage suite — packed-slot fuzzing,
struct depth, short bytes/string, and the `enable_packed_slots` paths.
`forge fmt --check` is clean.

---
🤖 Written with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code). All output
above is from a local `forge test` run.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit corrects incorrect handling of signed integer fields narrower than 256 bits in StdStorage (read, find, and checked_write). This fixes functional bugs but does not introduce or mitigate a security vulnerability in production code.

subject: test(StdJson): cover readBytes at parseRaw's inferred-type lengths (#900)
body:
## Motivation

Closes #592.

The reported bug — `readBytes` returning wrong data or reverting on
20-byte
values — does not reproduce on `master`. It was real on forge-std
v1.2.0, where
`readBytes` was `abi.decode(vm.parseJson(json, key), (bytes))`. It now
calls
`vm.parseJsonBytes` directly, which sidesteps the cause.

The cause itself is still there, one layer down. `parseRaw` infers a
value's
type instead of taking a declared one:

| hex string length | `parseRaw` output | inferred as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1, 19, 21, 31, 33 bytes | 96 bytes | dynamic `bytes` |
| **exactly 20 bytes** | 32 bytes | **`address`** |
| **exactly 32 bytes** | 32 bytes | **`bytes32`** |

So `abi.decode(json.parseRaw(key), (bytes))` still reverts at exactly 20
and 32
bytes. `readBytes` avoids it, but nothing in the suite says so —
`readBytes` has
no test coverage at all — and nothing in the docs warns about it.

## Solution

- `test_ReadBytesAtInferredTypeLengths` asserts `readBytes` round-trips
19, 20,
21, 31, 32 and 33 byte values, bracketing both inference boundaries. If
  `readBytes` is ever routed back through `parseRaw`, this fails.
- A `@dev` note on `parseRaw` documents the inference, so the next
person
  decoding its output as `bytes` knows why it reverts.

## Testing

`forge test`: 207 passing, 0 failing. `forge fmt --check` clean. Build
matrix
(stable, `--via-ir`, solc 0.8.13 and 0.8.35, each with and without IR)
all green.
rationale: The commit only adds a new test covering existing readBytes behavior and does not modify library code; it does not fix a bug nor address any security issue.

subject: fix(StdConfig): escape strings written back to the config file (#933)
body:
## Motivation

When `StdConfig` writes updates back to the TOML file, strings pass
through `_quote`, which only wraps them in double quotes:

```solidity
return string.concat('"', s, '"');
```

Nothing is escaped, so a string with `"`, `\` or a control character
reaches `vm.writeToml` as invalid JSON, or as different JSON, and the
file ends up with something other than what was `set`. With the new
test's values, the file on `master` contains:

```toml
quoted = '"say "hi""'          # the JSON didn't parse, so the quotes became part of the value
path = """
C:\tmp
ew"""                          # `\t` and `\n` in "C:\tmp\new" were read as escapes
escaped_array = """
["say "hi"","line one
line two"]"""                  # a string[] stored as a single string
```

No error is raised, and `config.get()` keeps returning the right value
from memory, so the problem only shows up on the next run. The values
come back altered, and `escaped_array` now has type `string`. The next
load would therefore type it `string` instead of `string[]`, and
`toStringArray()` would revert with `TypeMismatch`.

## Solution

`_quote` now encodes the value as a JSON string literal: it escapes `"`
and `\`, and writes control characters as `\u00XX`. Every string-valued
setter goes through `_quote`: `string`, `string[]`, and the hex strings
for `address`, `bytes32` and `bytes`, which contain nothing to escape.
So this one change covers all of them.

## Tests

`test_writeConfigEscapesStrings` writes a quoted string, a Windows-style
path and a multi-line string (as a scalar and inside a `string[]`), then
parses the file back. It fails on `master` (`"say "hi"" != say "hi"`)
and passes with the change.

Locally:
- `forge test` passes, except `testFuzz_PublicKey`, which needs a
cheatcode newer than my local forge (1.5.1).
- `forge build --contracts 'test/compilation/*'` passes with solc
0.8.13, with and without `--via-ir`.
- `forge fmt --check` is clean on both changed files.

Written with AI assistance (Claude Code).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

rationale: The commit corrects StdConfig's string quoting logic, fixing malformed TOML output that previously caused type mismatches on subsequent loads. This is a functional bug fix in test configuration handling, not a vulnerability exploitable to affect funds, keys, or contract execution.

subject: fix(StdSecp256k1): reject non-canonical coordinates in isOnCurve (#928)
body:
## Motivation

`StdSecp256k1.isOnCurve(x, y)` only compares `y² mod P` with `x³ + 7 mod
P`, so it also returns `true` for non-canonical coordinates `x >= P` or
`y >= P` that are congruent to a curve point. For example, `(1 + P, y)`
is accepted because `(1, y)` is on the curve.

This disagrees with the go-ethereum function referenced in the code
(`crypto/secp256k1/curve.go`, `IsOnCurve`), which returns `false` when
`x >= P || y >= P`. It also disagrees with the library's own docs
("Affine coordinates `(x, y)` are canonically in `[0, P)`") and with
`isIdentityProjective`, which already requires `y < P`. If a test
validates a public key with `isOnCurve`, a value like `(x, y + P)`
passes, and `toAddress` then gives a different address.

## Solution

Return `false` from `isOnCurve` when either coordinate is not in `[0,
P)`, and say so in the natspec. Add a test with two on-curve points (`x
= 1`, and a point with `y = 1`) where adding `P` to one coordinate still
fits in `uint256`. Before the change, the new test fails with `assertion
failed`. After the change, it passes. `forge fmt --check` is clean on
the touched files.

I used an AI assistant (Claude) while preparing this. I reproduced the
issue and checked the fix and tests myself.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Co-authored-by: Matthias Seitz <matthias.seitz@outlook.de>
rationale: The change adds canonical range checks to StdSecp256k1.isOnCurve, fixing a bug where non‑canonical coordinates (x >= P or y >= P) were incorrectly accepted as on‑curve. This could be exploited to validate malformed public keys that map to a different address, enabling identity spoofing and potential fund loss. The fix prevents that, making it a security‑relevant bug fix.

subject: fix for short address attack
body:
as suggested by /u/izqui9 here https://www.reddit.com/r/ethereum/comments/63s917/worrysome_bug_exploit_with_erc20_token/dfwmhc3/
Attack description: 
https://blog.golemproject.net/how-to-find-10m-by-just-reading-blockchain-6ae9d39fcd95
rationale: The diff adds an onlyPayloadSize modifier asserting msg.data.length equals the full ABI-encoded size (4-byte selector + 2*32) on transfer, which directly mitigates the ERC20 short-address attack where truncated calldata causes the EVM to zero-fill the address and shift _value higher, enabling over-transfer by a malicious caller. This guards fund transfers against attacker-controlled malformed input, so it is a security fix, though exploitation requires a third-party caller (e.g., an exchange) relaying the request.

subject: Signature Malleability: (#1622)
body:
* Transaction Malleability:
If you allow for both values 0/1 and 27/28, you allow two different
signatures both resulting in a same valid recovery. (r,s,0/1) and
(r,s,27/28) would both be valid, recover the same public key and sign
the same data. Furthermore, given (r,s,0/1), (r,s,27/28) can be
constructed by anyone.

* Transaction Malleability:
EIP-2 still allows signature malleabality for ecrecover(), remove this
possibility and force the signature to be unique.

* Added a reference to appendix F to the yellow paper and improved
comment.

* better test description for testing the version 0, which returns
a zero address

* Check that the conversion from 0/1 to 27/28 only happens if its 0/1

* improved formatting

* Refactor ECDSA code a bit.

* Refactor ECDSA tests a bit.

* Add changelog entry.

* Add high-s check test.
rationale: The diff adds a check rejecting s-values above half the curve order (0x7FFF...20A0) and removes the v += 27 normalization so only v=27/28 are accepted, enforcing EIP-2 signature uniqueness. Previously, anyone could flip s (or use v=0/1) to produce a second valid signature for the same hash, breaking contracts that rely on signature uniqueness for replay protection or authentication — a real, attacker-triggerable cryptographic signature issue.

subject: Update ReentrancyGuard for Istanbul Hard Fork (#1992)
body:
* Update ReentrancyGuard for Istanbul Hard Fork

Changes:
Added L37, `_guardCounter = 1;`

Rationale:
The planned _Istanbul Hard Fork_ will implement [EIP 2200](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/blob/e4d4ea348e06c54d0075c400dc7b72430d427ff1/EIPS/eip-2200.md), which implements "net gas metering" for `sstore` operations. If the final value of `_guardCounter` is unchanged relative to the original value of it, a gas refund will be applied and charges for changing the value of `_guardCounter` will effectively not exist. This ends up being cheaper than the current implementation ONLY AFTER Istanbul. Before Istanbul, the added line actually ends up costing more gas.

Note that if `_guardCounter` is `0` initially, the initial cost and subsequent refund will both be larger than if `_guardCounter` is `1` initially. Although in both cases, the net gas cost (`gasCost - gasRefund`) are equal, it's better in terms of cost to have both the gas cost and refund smaller, as there is some limit to the percentage of a gas refund that can actually be realized.

* Update CHANGELOG.md

Added note for change to ReentrancyGuard.sol

* Update ReentrancyGuard.sol

* Update CHANGELOG.md
rationale: The added `_guardCounter = 1;` line only resets the private guard counter after the require check so that Istanbul's EIP-2200 net-gas-metering refunds apply; it is a gas optimization for the hard fork, not a correction of incorrect behaviour. The reentrancy check logic (`localCounter == _guardCounter` after `_;`) is untouched and was already sound, and the counter reset occurs after all external calls, so no exploitable path is introduced or removed.

subject: Replace immutable with constant for _PERMIT_TYPEHASH (#3196)

This commit is related to the following issue discussion: https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/contracts-wizard/issues/89#issuecomment-1042391318

subject: ERC4626 inflation attack mitigation (#3979)
body: Co-authored-by: Francisco <fg@frang.io>

The changeset and the new attack-documentation diagrams in the diff corroborate that this corrects exploitable behaviour rather than adding an unrelated feature.

rationale: The diff adds `require(proofPos == proofLen, "MerkleProof: invalid multiproof")` in both `processMultiProof` and `processMultiProofCalldata`, closing a gap where proofs not fully consumed were accepted, allowing forged multiproofs (arbitrary leaves) via a zero-value node at depth 1; the changeset and bundled regression test confirm this is the GHSA-wprv-93r4-jj2p issue, which lets attackers bypass MerkleProof allowlists and claim unauthorized assets.

subject: Detect MerkleProof multiproof invariant violation (#4367)
body: Co-authored-by: Hadrien Croubois <hadrien.croubois@gmail.com>
rationale: The diff adds a proof-consumption invariant check (`proofPos != proofLen` reverts) in both `processMultiProof` and `processMultiProofCalldata`; the new test demonstrates a forged multiproof against a tree containing a zero node at depth 1, and the changeset states the pre-fix code allowed proving arbitrary leaves — a cryptographic proof-forgery/authorization bypass, exploitable where attackers can influence tree contents.

subject: Change release cycle `prBackExists` definition (#4365)

The new code fails gracefully with a diagnostic message. However, this is test-only infrastructure with no attacker-reachable or fund-affecting path, so it is not a security fix.

The removal of a redundant abstract contract plus a major-version changeset indicates a refactor/deprecation, not a correction of wrong behaviour.

rationale: The commit only removes an entry from a tooling annotation comment and makes no functional changes to contract code; it does not correct any misbehavior, nor does it address a security issue.

A single saved SLOAD in an internal view function is neither attacker-inducible nor fund/availability-affecting, so it is not a security fix.

subject: Add `GovernorTimelockControl` address to `TimelockController` salt (#4432)
body: Co-authored-by: Francisco Giordano <fg@frang.io>
rationale: The change fixes a collision bug where different Governor contracts using the same TimelockController could generate identical operation IDs (hashOperationBatch) when using only the description hash as salt, allowing one governor to interfere with another's queued actions. Adding the Governor address to the salt prevents this, addressing a security vulnerability.

subject: Fix invalid length check in SignatureChecker (#5973)
body: Signed-off-by: Hadrien Croubois <hadrien.croubois@gmail.com>
rationale: The change tightens the return‑data length check from >0x19 (25) to >0x1f (31) bytes, ensuring a full 32‑byte selector is returned before comparing it. Previously a contract could return fewer bytes and still pass the check, allowing signature validation bypass. This fixes an input‑validation bug that could be exploited to spoof signatures.

subject: Fix invalid length check in SignatureChecker (#5973)

subject: Optimize Math.average with unchecked math (#6019)
body: Co-authored-by: Ernesto García <ernestognw@gmail.com>
rationale: The arithmetic is provably overflow-free: (a & b) and (a ^ b) have disjoint bits so (a & b) + (a ^ b) = a | b fits in uint256, and (a ^ b)/2 ≤ (a ^ b), with no subtraction possible. Wrapping it in `unchecked` therefore changes no return value for any input — it is a pure gas optimization, not a bug fix or security fix.

subject: Use Math.mulDiv in ERC2981.royaltyInfo to avoid overflow on large salePrice (#6635)
rationale: The diff replaces `(salePrice * royaltyFraction) / _feeDenominator()` with overflow-safe `Math.mulDiv`; under Solidity 0.8 the old expression panics (reverts) when `salePrice * royaltyFraction` exceeds 2^256, so `royaltyInfo` could revert on very large salePrice values or small custom fee denominators, breaking royalty-aware sale flows (an availability/DoS issue, not fund loss). Practical exploitability is low since attacker-reachable salePrice values rarely reach the overflow threshold, hence Low severity.

subject: Use Math.mulDiv in ERC2981.royaltyInfo to avoid overflow on large salePrice (#6635)

subject: Test crosschain contracts against two simulated chains
body:
The ERC-7786 crosschain suites used to run both sides of a message on a
single chain, with `ERC7786GatewayMock.sendMessage` delivering to the
recipient synchronously. That made the "remote" side indistinguishable
from the local one: a single transaction carried the source and
destination events, and nothing exercised the chain boundary.

Each suite now spins up one `network.create()` per chain and relays
messages between them:

- `ERC7786GatewayMock.sendMessage` only emits `MessageSent`. Delivery
  happens through the new `relayMessage`, which an offchain relayer
  calls on the gateway deployed on the destination chain.
- `ERC7786Bridge` (test/helpers/erc7786.js) deploys a mock gateway per
  chain, scans them for messages sent since the previous pass, and
  delivers them on their destination -- cascading through messages a
  delivery itself triggers. It also provides a multichain `loadFixture`,
  since `networkHelpers.loadFixture` only snapshots its own connection.

Assertions now split at the chain boundary: source-side events on the
sending transaction, destination-side events on the relayed one. The
`only counterpart can send a crosschain message` cases go through
`relayMessage` with a non-counterpart sender, which is closer to what
they claim to check than the previous local send was.

Covers BridgeERC20/721/1155, the ERC20/721/1155 `Crosschain` token
extensions, ERC7786Recipient, CrosschainRemoteExecutor and
GovernorCrosschain.
rationale: Every substantive change is test infrastructure: test behavior files, test helpers, the test-only ERC7786GatewayMock, and a testing-conventions doc; no production contract logic is modified. Making the mock relay across two simulated chains improves test realism/coverage but does not correct wrong behaviour in shipped code, so it is a test-only change rather than a bug or security fix.

subject: Fix L-03: convert partial delay claims at the live rate
body:
Partial claims in ERC7540DelayDeposit and ERC7540DelayRedeem scaled the
already-rounded max* limits, rounding a second time. Convert the claimed
amount directly instead. Claiming the full limit still consumes the whole
claimable amount, so no dust is left behind.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The change fixes double‑rounding in partial claim conversions that could let users claim slightly more shares/assets than entitled, leading to token over‑issuance. This corrects a monetary accounting bug that could be exploited for profit, thus a security‑relevant fix.

subject: Fix L-13: report Admin request views only for requestId 0
body:
ERC7540AdminDeposit and ERC7540AdminRedeem aggregate all the Requests of a
controller under requestId 0, but their pending and claimable views ignored
the requestId and reported the same balance for any id. Return 0 for any
other requestId.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit changes _pendingDepositRequest, _claimableDepositRequest, _pendingRedeemRequest, and _claimableRedeemRequest to return values only for requestId 0, fixing the previous bug where any requestId returned the same balance. This corrects incorrect view logic but does not introduce or mitigate a security vulnerability.

subject: Fix M-03: document the donation attack on delay deposits
body:
Delay deposit claims are priced at the live rate, so a donation before a
claim lowers the shares it mints. Document the attack in the guide and in
the ERC7540DelayDeposit NatSpec, and recommend a non-zero _decimalsOffset.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit only adds documentation (NatSpec comments and guide text) about a known donation attack on delay deposits; no code behavior was changed, so it does not fix a bug nor address a security issue.

subject: Fix L-07: describe delay claims as controller or operator only
body:
The delay strategy NatSpec and guide said that anyone can claim once the
delay elapses. Requests mature automatically, but claims still require the
controller or one of its operators.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The commit only updates NatSpec comments and documentation to clarify that only the controller or its operators can claim, without changing any contract logic or behavior; therefore it is a documentation fix, not a bug fix or security fix.

subject: Fix L-01: document that request ids must be non-zero
body:
ERC-7540 reserves requestId 0 for strategies that aggregate the Requests
of a controller. Document that clock() and delay overrides in the delay
strategies, and current epoch overrides in the epoch strategies, must not
produce a zero id.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The diff contains only comment/blank-line changes across the four ERC-7540 files; no executable code was added or altered, so no pre-existing behaviour is corrected — this is a documentation clarification for implementers of delay/epoch overrides, not a bug fix.

subject: Fix L-09: document that a custom clock needs a matching CLOCK_MODE
body:
The delay strategies document overriding clock() to change the time
source, but the default CLOCK_MODE() reverts when the clock is not
block.timestamp. Document that both must be overridden together.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The diff contains only comment/blank-line additions to ERC7540DelayDeposit.sol and ERC7540DelayRedeem.sol documenting that custom clock() overrides need a matching CLOCK_MODE(); no executable behaviour changed, so nothing was corrected. A docs-only change is not a bug fix and therefore carries no security fix.

subject: Fix L-06: document the claimable view during out-of-order fulfillment
body:
When a newer epoch is fulfilled before an older one, the controller's
claims stay gated on the oldest Pending epoch. Document that the
per-epoch claimable view reports the newer epoch in the meantime, while
the max* limits do not include it yet.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The diff consists entirely of comment/blank-line changes documenting already-existing out-of-order fulfillment behavior; no executable code changed, so no behavior was corrected and there is no security impact.

subject: Fix L-11: document that max* overrides must keep the claimable ratio
body:
Admin claims are priced with the ratio between the max* limits of each
side, which default to the claimable pair locked at fulfillment. Document
that overrides must keep both limits at the same ratio.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
rationale: The diff changed only comments/documentation (the addressed L-11 audit item is resolved by documenting an override requirement), so no executable behaviour was corrected before/after and there is nothing an attacker could exploit differently.

subject: Signature Malleability: (#1622)
body:
* Transaction Malleability:
If you allow for both values 0/1 and 27/28, you allow two different
signatures both resulting in a same valid recovery. (r,s,0/1) and
(r,s,27/28) would both be valid, recover the same public key and sign
the same data. Furthermore, given (r,s,0/1), (r,s,27/28) can be
constructed by anyone.

* Transaction Malleability:
EIP-2 still allows signature malleabality for ecrecover(), remove this
possibility and force the signature to be unique.

* Added a reference to appendix F to the yellow paper and improved
comment.

* better test description for testing the version 0, which returns
a zero address

* Check that the conversion from 0/1 to 27/28 only happens if its 0/1

* improved formatting

* Refactor ECDSA code a bit.

* Refactor ECDSA tests a bit.

* Add changelog entry.

* Add high-s check test.
rationale: The commit changes ECDSA.recover to reject non‑canonical signatures (v values 0/1 and high‑s values) that previously were accepted, fixing a signature malleability bug that could be exploited to produce alternative valid signatures for the same data.

subject: Update ReentrancyGuard for Istanbul Hard Fork (#1992)
body:
* Update ReentrancyGuard for Istanbul Hard Fork

Changes:
Added L37, `_guardCounter = 1;`

Rationale:
The planned _Istanbul Hard Fork_ will implement [EIP 2200](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/blob/e4d4ea348e06c54d0075c400dc7b72430d427ff1/EIPS/eip-2200.md), which implements "net gas metering" for `sstore` operations. If the final value of `_guardCounter` is unchanged relative to the original value of it, a gas refund will be applied and charges for changing the value of `_guardCounter` will effectively not exist. This ends up being cheaper than the current implementation ONLY AFTER Istanbul. Before Istanbul, the added line actually ends up costing more gas.

Note that if `_guardCounter` is `0` initially, the initial cost and subsequent refund will both be larger than if `_guardCounter` is `1` initially. Although in both cases, the net gas cost (`gasCost - gasRefund`) are equal, it's better in terms of cost to have both the gas cost and refund smaller, as there is some limit to the percentage of a gas refund that can actually be realized.

* Update CHANGELOG.md

Added note for change to ReentrancyGuard.sol

* Update ReentrancyGuard.sol

* Update CHANGELOG.md
rationale: The change only adds a line resetting _guardCounter to 1 for gas‑cost reasons after the Istanbul hard fork; it does not alter functional behavior or fix a defect, nor does it address a security issue.

rationale: The commit removes the `confirmTransaction` flow and related code, changing the contract's behavior to no longer allow contract‑based confirmations. This appears to fix an access‑control issue where owners could bypass signature checks, a security‑relevant defect.

rationale: The change adds a missing version byte to the transaction hash used for signatures, correcting the hash calculation. Without this byte, signatures could be replayed or mis‑validated, a classic authentication/spoofing vulnerability.

subject: Adjusted extension logic
rationale: The commit adds a getGnosisSafe() accessor and enforces that extensions added to a GnosisSafe must reference the same safe (require(this == extension.getGnosisSafe())) and that executeExtension checks the same condition. This prevents malicious extensions from being attached to a safe and executed, fixing an improper access control bug that could allow arbitrary code execution and fund theft.

subject: Fixed tests
rationale: The commit changes the return type of getGnosisSafe from address to GnosisSafe and updates tests to use the corrected interface, fixing compilation/test failures. No security-relevant behavior is altered.

rationale: The diff refactors executeDailyLimit into an internal executeInternal with identical checks (require(gnosisSafe.isOwner(sender)) replacing the msg.sender check via parameter passing) and adds a new signature-based entry point (DailyLimitExtensionWithSignature) plus tests, implementing feature request #14 rather than correcting prior wrong behaviour; the visible code shows no defect being fixed in existing logic.

subject: Implements #20: Optimize array access in setup functions
rationale: All three files only hoist the repeated array element reads (_owners[i], _friends[i], accounts[i]) into a local variable; the array parameters are immutable within the call, so the checks, mapping writes, and observable behaviour are identical before and after — a pure gas optimization, not a defect correction, hence no security impact.

subject: Use gas instead of not(0)
rationale: The commit replaces the use of not(0) (an all‑bits‑set constant) with the gas opcode for the gas argument of call/delegatecall. Using not(0) can lead to out‑of‑gas failures under EIP‑150's 63/64 gas forwarding rule, potentially causing calls to revert and enabling denial‑of‑service attacks. Changing to gas corrects this behavior.

subject: replace assembly switch with if
rationale: All three edits convert `switch X case 0 { revert } [default ...]` into `if eq(X, 0) { revert }` plus fall-through logic; since call/delegatecall return only 0 or 1, revert-on-failure and return/no-op-on-success behavior is semantically identical before and after. This is a style refactor (likely silencing solc warnings about switch on bool), with no behavioral change to fix.

subject: Mask Immutables in Local Verify Task (#691)
body:
Fixes #689

The local verification task does not work correctly for contracts with
`immutable`s. This is because, `immutable` values get written when the
contract's init code executes on-chain, but uses `0` place holders in
the `deployedBytecode` compiler output.

This causes the code that is fetched from the deployed contract to
differ slightly from the compiler's byte code output (fetched code has
non-0 `immutable` values, while the compiler output has 0 `immutable`
values).

The fix is to mask the `immutable`s from the fetched code with 0's
before comparing.

With this fix, `local-verify` script now works for the
`SimulateTxAccessor` contract:

```
$ npx hardhat local-verify --network localhost
Verification status for CompatibilityFallbackHandler: SUCCESS
Verification status for CreateCall: SUCCESS
Verification status for MultiSend: SUCCESS
Verification status for MultiSendCallOnly: SUCCESS
Verification status for Safe: SUCCESS
Verification status for SafeL2: SUCCESS
Verification status for SafeProxyFactory: SUCCESS
Verification status for SignMessageLib: SUCCESS
Verification status for SimulateTxAccessor: SUCCESS
Verification status for TokenCallbackHandler: SUCCESS
```
rationale: The diff corrects a tooling defect in the local-verify task: before the fix, comparing fetched on-chain code (with real immutable values) against compiler output (zero placeholders) produced false FAILURE results for contracts with immutables, which the fix resolves by zeroing immutableReferences before hashing. subject: enableModule require -> if with revert (saves 2 bytes)
rationale: The diff is a pure De Morgan rewrite: `require(module != 0 && module != SENTINEL, "GS101")` becomes `if (module == 0 || module == SENTINEL) revert("GS101")`, which reverts on exactly the same inputs with the identical error string (and `revert("...")` is semantically identical to `require(false, "...")`). This is a bytecode-size/gas optimization with no observable behaviour change, so it is not a bug fix and has no security consequence.

subject: disableModule require -> if with revert (saves 2 bytes)
rationale: The change is a logically equivalent rewrite via De Morgan's law: `require(!(A && B))` and `if (A || B) revert` revert with the identical 'GS101' message under exactly the same conditions, so there is no behaviour change — only a bytecode-size/gas optimization as the subject states. Since pre-fix behaviour was correct and unchanged, this is neither a bug fix nor a security fix.

Add Safe to L2 Setup Contract (#759)
body:
This PR introduces a setup contract that can be called from the `Safe`
setup function in order to automatically promote a Safe at setup time if
the code is executing on an L2. Namely, this allows the Safe Proxy
factory to use a single singleton and initializer for all chains, but
end up with different `singleton`s depending on the chain ID.

The expected use of this contract is to use the standard proxy factory:

```solidity
Safe l1Singleton;
SafeL2 l2Singleton;
SafeToL2Setup l2Setup;

proxyFactory.createProxyWithNonce(
    address(l1Singleton),
    abi.encodeCall(
        l1Singleton.setup,
        (
            owners,
            threshold,
            address(l2Setup),
            abi.encodeCall(l2Setup.setupToL2, address(l2Singleton)),
            fallbackHandler,
            paymentToken,
            payment,
            paymentReceiver
        )
    ),
    saltNonce
)
```

On L1 (i.e. Ethereum Mainnet where `chainId == 1`), you would end up
with a Safe where `safe.singleton == l1Singleton` and on any other
chains, you would end up with `safe.singleton == l2Singleton`. This
would happen _before_ the first transaction.

---------

Co-authored-by: Mikhail <16622558+mmv08@users.noreply.github.com>
rationale: The diff's only substantive code is a brand-new contract, SafeToL2Setup.sol, which adds the ability to swap the Safe singleton to the L2 variant during setup when chainId != 1, plus supporting tests and build/CI config tweaks; it introduces new functionality rather than correcting any previously wrong behaviour, so it is neither a bug fix nor a security fix.

subject: Generic migration contract (#793)
body:
Fixes: #787 

## Summary

This PR adds a general migration contract that takes address of the
Safe, SafeL2 and fallback handler contracts during deployment. The
contract allows Safe to update the Singleton at `address(0)`.

- Uses error strings rather than error types because Solidity version
0.7.6 doesn't support it.

As of now tests cover below migration paths: 
- 1.3.0 to 1.5.0
- 1.3.0 to 1.4.1
- 14.1 to 1.5.0

See `SafeMigration.spec.ts` to see how tests are organised. Do share if
you any thoughts to better run same tests on different migration paths.

The migration contract stores address of the Safe singletons and
fallback handler rather than using code hash and requiring the user to
provide singleton address as described in the issue. The reason being as
follows:
 
Checking codehash of the target singleton means user has to provide the
address of the target singleton. Also, checking code hash has higher gas
costs.

The only argument for using code hash for upgrades is that it also
allows unofficial singletons to be used for migration using official
migration contract. But, users/projects can also deploy their own
version of migration contract by providing singleton addresses in the
constructor and have similar security guarantees as the official
migration contract.

## Changes in PR
- Create a general migration contract which is not tightly bound to any
specific Safe version
- Update tests
- Remove other migration contract as this PR supersedes it
 
Unlike `Safe150Migration.sol`, this new contract does not check if
slot(0) of the contract stores an address having some non-empty code. I
think this check is not need because this contract is not intended to be
used in general by other proxy contracts and checking slot(0) value is
only a partially correct way. Would like to know thought of others.

---------

Co-authored-by: Shebin John <admin@remedcu.com>
Co-authored-by: Mikhail <16622558+mmv08@users.noreply.github.com>
rationale: The diff adds a new generic SafeMigration contract (with constructor-supplied singleton/fallback-handler addresses) and deletes the version-specific migration contracts it supersedes, updating tests accordingly — a generalization/feature replacement rather than a correction of wrong behavior. The only behavioral relaxation (dropping Safe150Migration's slot(0) code check) is an intentional design simplification argued in the message, not a fix for an exploitable defect, and the heavily truncated diff shows no attacker-inducible bug being corrected.

rationale: The diff is purely additive: it introduces a new ProxyCreationL2 event and wrapper functions (createProxyWithNonceL2, createProxyWithCallbackL2) that delegate to the unchanged existing functions, purely to improve indexability of creation data. No prior incorrect behaviour is corrected, and no data is disclosed that is not already public in the deployment transaction calldata, so this is a feature, not a security fix.

subject: optimize `getTransactionHash` by implementing it in assembly (#847)
body:
This pull request includes significant changes to the `Safe` contract
and its associated test suite. The changes focus on optimizing the
encoding of transaction data and enhancing the test coverage for
transaction hash calculations.

### Optimizations in `Safe` contract:

*
[`contracts/Safe.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-587b494ea631bb6b7adf4fc3e1a2e6a277a385ff16e1163b26e39de24e9483deL414-R467):
Rewrote the transaction data encoding logic in assembly to avoid
multiple memory allocations, improving gas efficiency.

### Enhancements in test suite:

*
[`test/core/Safe.Signatures.spec.ts`](diffhunk://#diff-d7bc3771858069f85022d38344b6cb5302146da4bafde1ac18910e3d7bfac43bL49-R56):
Enhanced the test case for calculating EIP-712 hash by introducing a
loop to generate and test multiple random transactions.
[[1]](diffhunk://#diff-d7bc3771858069f85022d38344b6cb5302146da4bafde1ac18910e3d7bfac43bL49-R56)
[[2]](diffhunk://#diff-d7bc3771858069f85022d38344b6cb5302146da4bafde1ac18910e3d7bfac43bR72).
The previous test case was inefficient as it contained empty safe
transaction data. The test would still pass if you forgot to include it
in hashing.
* I also added a FV rule to verify hash computation correctness.

### Benchmarks

#### Before
```
  ERC20 - transfer
           Used 51800n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with an EOA (137ms)
           Used 82980n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a single owner Safe
           Used 88874n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a single owner and guard Safe
           Used 90024n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a 2 out of 2 Safe
           Used 97094n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a 3 out of 3 Safe
           Used 97094n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a 3 out of 5 Safe
```    

#### After

```
ERC20 - transfer
           Used 51800n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with an EOA (71ms)
           Used 82494n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a single owner Safe
           Used 88375n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a single owner and guard Safe
           Used 89547n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a 2 out of 2 Safe
           Used 96577n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a 3 out of 3 Safe
           Used 96589n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a 3 out of 5 Safe
```

On average, it saves ~485 gas, not much, but considering this is the
hottest path, it should result in significant accumulated savings.
(After 44 Safe transactions, a user would save 21k gas - enough for
broadcasting a native token transfer)

### Codesize

It saves 273 bytes in code size.

#### Before
SafeL2 22582 bytes (limit is 24576)

#### After

SafeL2 22309 bytes (limit is 24576)
rationale: The commit changes the getTransactionHash implementation and its visibility, fixing a previous omission in the hash calculation that could allow incorrect transaction hashes to be signed. This directly impacts signature verification, a security-critical operation, and the added tests highlight the prior weakness.

subject: Assembly Memory Safety (#859)
body:
This PR does a once-over on memory Safety for the 1.5.0 contracts. In
particular, there were a couple of missing `memory-safe` tags for some
assembly blocks which were preventing the IR assembler from working
correctly.

Additionally, since the `MultiSend*` contracts changed anyway in 1.5.0,
I took this opportunity to change the assembly to be memory-safe so that
we can tag it. Note that it only adds more code in the revert case, so
it should not have a negative impact for most use-cases.

Furthermore, I added a comment explaining why we did not make the
`SafeProxy` contract memory-safe (that is one intentional).

Lastly, I noticed that there were some `eq(..., 0)` assembly calls which
can be written as `iszero(...)` to save some gas and code. Again, it was
an opportunistic change as the affected contracts have changed anyway
and will be re-audited.

---------

Co-authored-by: Shebin John <admin@remedcu.com>
rationale: The commit adds missing `memory-safe` tags to assembly blocks and adjusts assembly code to be memory‑safe, fixing compilation/IR assembly issues. This corrects a bug but does not appear to address a security‑relevant vulnerability.

body:
Matter Labs recently renamed `era-test-node` to `zksync-anvil`. This
causes the official `hardhat-zksync-node` package to stop working.

It is possible to patch the NPM package so that it works with `sed`:

```sh
find node_modules/@matterlabs/hardhat-zksync-node/ -type f -exec sed -i "s/era[_-]test[_-]node/anvil-zksync/g" '{}' ';'
```

However, the tests seem to be quite flaky (ran on my machine once, but
the `anvil` node seems to crash quite often).
rationale: This is a test/CI maintenance commit: it removes the broken flaky 'test:zk' step from the default test script, ignores a new log file, adds --noPrompt to solhint --fix, and refactors test describe blocks/signer fixtures — no smart contract or runtime behaviour changes are present in the diff, so nothing previously wrong in the product is corrected.

body:
This pull request includes an important update to the `ERC165Handler`

code. The most significant changes are as follows:

### The following optimizes the logic and minimizes storage accesses:

*
[`contracts/handler/extensible/ERC165Handler.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-aa0838f20fd3f37b00dc661645b4641500e68762b9b624addb99465fcc65a3e0L38-R48):

subject: [Certora Audit] G-09. Cache array length outside of loop (#896)
body:
This pull request includes several optimizations to the `OwnerManager`
and `ERC165Handler` contracts by reducing the number of times array
lengths are accessed within loops. These changes aim to improve the
efficiency of the code by storing the array lengths in variables before
the loops.

If not cached, the solidity compiler will always read the length of the
array during each iteration. That is, if it is a storage array, this is
an extra sload operation (100 additional extra gas for each iteration
except for the first) and if it is a memory array, this is an extra
mload operation (3 additional gas for each iteration except for the
first).

Optimizations in `OwnerManager` contract:

*
[`contracts/base/OwnerManager.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-795fb06764b4c2d991707584a31509badf0b036c9401bfbcb82d6bc9fdebab82L38-R39):
Stored `_owners.length` in a variable `ownersLength` before the loop to
avoid repeatedly accessing the array length.
*
[`contracts/base/OwnerManager.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-795fb06764b4c2d991707584a31509badf0b036c9401bfbcb82d6bc9fdebab82L49-R50):
Updated `ownerCount` to use the `ownersLength` variable instead of
accessing `_owners.length` again.

Optimizations in `ERC165Handler` contract:

*
[`contracts/handler/extensible/ERC165Handler.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-aa0838f20fd3f37b00dc661645b4641500e68762b9b624addb99465fcc65a3e0L56-R57):
Stored `handlerWithSelectors.length` in a variable `len` before the loop
in `addSupportedInterfaceBatch` to avoid repeatedly accessing the array
length.
*
[`contracts/handler/extensible/ERC165Handler.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-aa0838f20fd3f37b00dc661645b4641500e68762b9b624addb99465fcc65a3e0L78-R80):
Stored `selectors.length` in a variable `len` before the loop in
`removeSupportedInterfaceBatch` to avoid repeatedly accessing the array
length.
rationale: The diff only caches array lengths (all calldata parameters, which cannot mutate during the call) before loops; iteration counts and resulting state (e.g., ownerCount = _owners.length) are identical before and after, so this is a pure gas optimization from a Certora audit, not a correction of incorrect behaviour.

subject: [Certora Audit] G-10. ++i costs less gas compared to i++ or i+=1 (#897)
body:
This pull request includes several changes to increment and decrement
operations in various Solidity contract files. The primary goal is to
decrease gas usage.

Pre-increments and pre-decrements are cheaper.
For a uint256 i variable, the following is true with the Optimizer
enabled at 10k:
Increment:
- i += 1 is the most expensive form
- i++ costs 6 gas less than i += 1
- ++i costs 5 gas less than i++ (11 gas less than i += 1)

Decrement:
- i -= 1 is the most expensive form
- i-- costs 11 gas less than i -= 1
- --i costs 5 gas less than i-- (16 gas less than i -= 1)

Changes to increment and decrement operations:

*
[`contracts/Safe.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-587b494ea631bb6b7adf4fc3e1a2e6a277a385ff16e1163b26e39de24e9483deL296-R296):
Updated the for loop to use the prefix increment operator in the `Safe`
contract.
*
[`contracts/base/ModuleManager.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-82762908b9416ddadffb149ee4d25f328078fc27f938d454d8a207aad1ec3839L215-R215):
Changed the increment operation to use the prefix increment operator in
the `ModuleManager` contract.
*
[`contracts/base/OwnerManager.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-795fb06764b4c2d991707584a31509badf0b036c9401bfbcb82d6bc9fdebab82L38-R38):
Multiple updates to use prefix increment and decrement operators in the
`OwnerManager` contract.
[[1]](diffhunk://#diff-795fb06764b4c2d991707584a31509badf0b036c9401bfbcb82d6bc9fdebab82L38-R38)
[[2]](diffhunk://#diff-795fb06764b4c2d991707584a31509badf0b036c9401bfbcb82d6bc9fdebab82L63-R63)
[[3]](diffhunk://#diff-795fb06764b4c2d991707584a31509badf0b036c9401bfbcb82d6bc9fdebab82L80-R80)
[[4]](diffhunk://#diff-795fb06764b4c2d991707584a31509badf0b036c9401bfbcb82d6bc9fdebab82L142-R142)
*
[`contracts/common/StorageAccessible.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-a7dd65d90b0567bb9ba14ecd4ff414529a934cd3752ccf309800fad93fba354eL19-R19):
Modified the for loop to use the prefix increment operator in the
`StorageAccessible` contract.
*
[`contracts/handler/extensible/ERC165Handler.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-aa0838f20fd3f37b00dc661645b4641500e68762b9b624addb99465fcc65a3e0L56-R56):

`ERC165Handler` contract.
[[1]](diffhunk://#diff-aa0838f20fd3f37b00dc661645b4641500e68762b9b624addb99465fcc65a3e0L56-R56)
[[2]](diffhunk://#diff-aa0838f20fd3f37b00dc661645b4641500e68762b9b624addb99465fcc65a3e0L78-R78)
*
[`contracts/libraries/SafeToL2Migration.sol`](diffhunk://#diff-925588b812f729cc164d14a48e571ce813e2f0ae6f5c5420fc0382c767287fd0L188-R188):
Changed the increment operation to use the prefix increment operator in
the `SafeToL2Migration` contract.
rationale: The diff only replaces post-increment/post-decrement with prefix operators in loop counters across six files; as standalone statements ++i and i++ are semantically identical, so this is a pure gas optimization with no behaviour change. The commit message itself frames it as an audit gas finding (G-10), and ~5-11 gas per iteration has no security consequence.

subject: [Certora Audit] G07. Use a mask instead of shifting left and right (#894)
body:
This pull request includes changes to the `contracts/handler/extensible`
directory, specifically in the `MarshalLib.sol` and
`SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol` files. The changes focus on improving the
handling of data and selectors within assembly code blocks to decrease

bitwise AND operation to ensure proper extraction of the handler

[[1]](diffhunk://#diff-7122c44132b6fc89cd7c9f3c48519c88aaf7308705a1170d307d72465eb9e1c9L41-R41)
[[2]](diffhunk://#diff-7122c44132b6fc89cd7c9f3c48519c88aaf7308705a1170d307d72465eb9e1c9L59-R59)

/ MUL` opcode uses 5 gas, the `SHR / SHL` opcode only uses 3 gas.

operation `<< 6` to reduce gas costs in the `gasleft` check.

Replaced the multiplication operation `* 32` with the bitwise shift
operation `<< 5` to reduce gas costs when creating a new bytes array.
rationale: The commit only replaces multiplication by powers of two with equivalent left‑shift operations for gas savings; this is a pure refactor with no change in functional behavior, so it does not fix a bug nor address a security issue.

ensures its inner `simulateAndRevert` reverts as expected. This is to

rationale: The commit modifies the CompatibilityFallbackHandler's simulate function to ensure the inner simulateAndRevert call actually reverts, preventing unintended state changes when the handler is invoked outside a Safe. This corrects a bug that could be exploited to alter contract state, a security-relevant issue.

subject: Ackee[M1]: Deprecate `createProxyWithCallback` Function (#955)
body:
It is possible to front-run a `createProxyWithCallback` deployment using
`createProxyWithNonce` with a crafted `saltNonce`. This would make it so
the proxy would be deployed, but the callback not executed. Since this
method is not in use, we are deciding to deprecate it.

Alternatively, it would be possible to bring it back by using a
different `CREATE2` salt computation method in case this method is
needed in the future. Integrations that require a specific call at
deployment call can use the `setup` parameters with a `to` and `data`,
which would guarantee a callback at deployment time.
rationale: The diff removes `createProxyWithCallback`/`createProxyWithCallbackL2`, whose deterministic salt `keccak256(abi.encodePacked(saltNonce, callback))` let an attacker front-run the deployment by calling `createProxyWithNonce` with that same salt, deploying the proxy without ever invoking the callback — an attacker-inducible race (TOCTOU/front-running) violating expected deployment behavior. Removing the vulnerable entry point eliminates the race, so this is a security-motivated fix, though impact is capped by the fact the function was unused.

subject: Ackee[L1]: Verify ERC-165 Conformance (#956)
body:
ERC-165 requires that the `supportsInterface` implementation use less
than 30.000 gas. This PR adds an additional unit test to ensure that the
extensible fallback handler meets this requirement.
rationale: The diff touches only test/handlers/ExtensibleFallbackHandler.spec.ts, adding a gas-benchmark contract and a unit test asserting supportsInterface stays under 30,000 gas; no contract code is changed, so no pre-existing wrong behaviour is corrected. Since the added test presumably passes against the unchanged handler, this is a compliance/regression test, not a bug fix or security fix.

body:

`checkNSignatures` backwards compatible method is (Safe) and adds a
backwards compatible `encodeTransactionData` method to the
`CompatibilityFallbackHandler`.
rationale: The commit restores a backwards-compatible `encodeTransactionData` view helper (plus its SAFE_TX_TYPEHASH constant) to the CompatibilityFallbackHandler and fixes CHANGELOG statements about where `checkNSignatures` lives; this fixes the absence of the v1.x-compatible API expected by off-chain integrations, which is a compatibility defect but only a functional one. The added function is a stateless view computation over `msg.sender`'s domainSeparator, so the pre-fix behaviour (a revert or missing method) has no attacker-inducible or fund/availability impact shown in the diff.

subject: Ackee[L3]: Mask `masterCopy` Selector (#960)
body:
This PR changes the proxy implementation slightly to mask the
`masterCopy` selector instead of assuming that the trailing bytes are 0.
This makes the `masterCopy()` handling Solidity ABI conformant. Without
this change, the `masterCopy` function would not be able to be used
behind an ERC-2771 trusted forwarder for example.
rationale: The change masks extra calldata bytes when checking the `masterCopy` selector, fixing a bug where non‑zero trailing bytes caused the proxy to treat the call as a fallback delegatecall. This could be exploited to bypass the intended view function and trigger unintended delegatecalls, a classic input‑validation issue.

subject: Ackee[W1]: Less Confusing Event Emission (#973)
body:
We simplified the `ExtensibleFallbackHandler` to use a single event,
instead of selecting an event depending on the parameters. This makes
the events more consistent with the other Safe contract events, namely:

- We roughly emit one event per method (so, `setFallbackHandler` or
`setGuard` also do not distinguish between enabling and disabling, while
`addOwner` and `removeOwner` do)
- We consistently emit an event regardless of whether or not the storage
actually changed.
rationale: The commit only changes event emission and storage handling to always emit a single Changed event and sets removed entries to zero instead of deleting them, which is a refactor for clarity rather than fixing incorrect behavior; no security-relevant logic is altered.

subject: Ackee[W2]: Safe to L2 Migration Adjustments (#961)
body:
This PR changes the `SafeToL2Migration` contract to use `msg.data`
internally instead of re-computing the calldata. We also document that
the accuracy of the `SafeMultiSigTransaction` event data is best-effort
only, highlighting some possible senarios where it may be inaccurate.
rationale: The change fixes incorrect reconstruction of calldata for the SafeMultiSigTransaction event by using msg.data directly, correcting event data accuracy. No evidence that the prior behavior could be exploited to compromise security.

subject: Ackee[W3]: Clear High `masterCopy` Bits (#962)
body:
This PR changes the `SafeProxy` to write to the Solidity zero slot
instead of the scratch space. This ensures that the leading bits to the
encoded `masterCopy` value is guaranteed to be zero. While they
currently are 0 for all versions of Solidity that the code supports
(0.7.6 -> 0.8.30), this makes the code future-proof to potential
Compiler changes that may make the scratch space start dirty before
entering the `fallback` method.
rationale: The diff changes the memory location used to return the masterCopy address, moving from a scratch slot that may contain leftover high bits to a zeroed slot, fixing a bug where uninitialized memory could affect the returned address. This prevents potential misuse or leakage of unintended data, a security-relevant issue.

subject: Ackee[W4]: `SafeSetup` Outdated Event Parameters (#963)
body:
We document that the `SafeSetup` may emit an event with outdated
parameters if the initializer `DELEGATECALL` modifies any of them on the
Safe.
rationale: The commit moves the SafeSetup event emission before storage‑modifying delegate calls, fixing a bug where the event could contain outdated parameters. Incorrect event data can mislead users about owners/threshold, constituting a spoofing security issue.

subject: Ackee[W6]: Prevent `TokenCallbackHandler` from Locking Tokens (#965)
body:
This PR changes the implementation of `TokenCallbackHandler` and
`TokenCallbacks` to make a best-effort check on whether the tokens were
sent to a Safe that configures a token callback handler contract as a
fallback handler, or if it sent to the fallback handler contract itself
directly.

Thanks @remedcu and @rmeissner for the suggestions on how to implement
it! Basically, it works calling the `msg.sender` and expecting it to be
a Safe configured with the fallback handler. This would either:

- Fail if the token doesn't implement `StorageAccessible`
- Fail if the token doesn't have the specific `FALLBACK_HANDLER_SLOT`
set to the actual fallback handler

Note, however, that it is possible to trick the fallback handler into
receiving tokens. Because of this, we document that the checks are
best-effort only! We add a test to document how the fallback handler can
be tricked.
rationale: The commit adds a best‑effort check in TokenCallbackHandler (and related contracts) to ensure tokens are only sent to a Safe configured with a fallback handler, preventing tokens from being locked in the fallback handler contract. This corrects a previously exploitable behavior that could cause permanent loss of user funds.

subject: Ackee[I2]: Make `ISafe` Payable (#967)
body:

receive tokens. This PR adds a `INativeCurrencyPaymentFallback`
interface with a payable `receive` function and makes the `ISafe`
interface inherit from it. This makes the `ISafe` interface payable, and
requires addresses that are cast to it to also be `payable`.
rationale: The change makes the ISafe interface payable by inheriting a receive() payable function and updates casts to payable, fixing a functional issue where the Safe contract could not correctly receive native currency. No evidence of an exploitable security vulnerability is present.

subject: Deprecate `SafeToL2Migration` (#1008)
body:
The `SafeToL2Migration` contract was previously included in the Safe
v1.5.0 release, but it had not been modified to work with the Safe
v1.5.0 contracts. In particular, the version string "1.5.0" had not been
allow-listed by the contract for migrations.

The `SafeToL2Migration` contract is written in such a way that it
requires that the version of the L1 singleton matches the L2 singleton
for the migration to succeed. As such, adding support for the 1.5.0
singletons would have arguably very limited benefit, as all recent Safes
are created with the `SafeToL2Setup` contract in order to ensure
consistent addresses across Ethereum Mainnet and L2s (which use a
different singleton). As such, there should be no new Safes created by
the Safe{Wallet} interface that would require migration, and therefore,
there would be no v1.5.0 Safes created by the interface that would
require migration, making the contract no longer useful for future
versions. **Therefore, we have chosen to deprecate the
`SafeToL2Migration` contract for the 1.5.0 release**.

There is the possibility of adding migration contract from Safes with
singleton version `X.Y.Z+L1` to `1.5.0+L2`, but without clear
requirements, it does not have to be added now or affect the release of
the 1.5.0 contracts.
rationale: The commit removes the broken `SafeToL2Migration` contract and related CI/spec files, correcting the inclusion of non‑functional code. No security‑relevant behavior is altered, so it is not a security fix.

body:
We give it the same treatment as `getTransactionHash`, as it has
sufficiently substantial gains IMO, and the assembly is simple enough.

**Before:**

```
$ npm run codesize | grep '^Safe '
Safe 21434 bytes (limit is 24576)

$ npm run benchmark | grep -A4 'ERC20 - transfer' | sed '1P;$!N;$!D'
  ERC20 - transfer
           Used 82498n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a single owner Safe
```

**After:**

```
$ npm run codesize | grep '^Safe '
Safe 21372 bytes (limit is 24576)

$ npm run benchmark | grep -A4 'ERC20 - transfer' | sed '1P;$!N;$!D'
  ERC20 - transfer
           Used 82382n gas for >transfer<
    ✔ with a single owner Safe
```
rationale: This is a pure gas/codesize refactor: both versions compute keccak256 over DOMAIN_SEPARATOR_TYPEHASH, chainid, and the contract address with identical 32-byte/zero-padded encoding (mstore of an address places it in the low-order bytes, matching abi.encode's address padding), so the returned domainSeparator is unchanged. The commit message confirms the motivation is benchmark/codesize gains, not a behavioral correction.

subject: Allow Safe to Own Itself (#998)
body:
This change was originally proposed by @akshay-ap 

This PR reverts an old change (See #229 and #259) and allows the Safe to
once again own itself. This is a step towards 7702 support (#997),
whereby we want the EOA that delegates to a Safe to be able to sign
transactions for itself.

The restriction was originally put in place because `execTransaction`
would call `isValidSignature` on itself (which used to be implemented on
the Safe itself and not as part of the compatibility fallback handler),
where the `msg.sender` would be the Safe itself, and allow for trivial
"approved hash" signatures (through

[this](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-smart-account/blob/36db12a140331c522e773849ebc87d39f5abae1e/contracts/GnosisSafe.sol#L244-L245)
mechanism).

This is no longer possible since v1.3.0, as the `isValidSignature` call
would be handled by the fallback handler, meaning that the `msg.sender`
that can trivially sign "approve hash" signatures is no longer the Safe
itself but the configured fallback handler. Since #866 and starting in
v1.5.0 the `CompatibilityFallbackHandler` is implemented to disallow
"approve hash" signatures regardless of the caller, further eliminating
the requirement for the restriction.

### Increasing Threshold Concerns

One concern with this change, and removing the restriction on having the
Safe own itself, is that the Safe cannot sign for itself, so you can
potentially block access to the account completely, by requiring the
Safe "self-owner" to be included as part of the signing threshold. For
example, if you have a n/n Safe (so `threshold == ownerCount`) and one
of the owners is the Safe itself, then the Safe will not be able to ever
produce a valid signature.
rationale: The change removes the prohibition on a Safe being its own owner, adding a new capability rather than correcting erroneous behavior, and does not address a disclosed security vulnerability.

This PR changes the Safe smart account logic to disallow `owner == this`

to use Safe as a delegation target, but without leaving in the footgun
where users can accidentally add a non-EIP-7702 Safe as its own owner
and effectively reducing the owner count (since a contract-based Safe
cannot sign for itself) and allowing situations where it is not possible
for generate a threshold of sigantures.

Additionally, I moved some Solidity files around to better reflect the
project layout:
- `Enum.sol` goes to the `interfaces/` directory, since it is arguably
an interface type
- `ErrorMessage.sol` goes into `common/` as it is not a library in the
Safe core contracts meaning of the word.

Added tests around the new logic, and with the refactoring I did in the
`OwnerManager.sol`, the code size actually decreased with this PR, even
with the added feature :)

As a side note, the EIP-7702 tests are unfortunately disabled for
coverage, as they fail with:

```
ProviderError: Cannot send both gasPrice and authorizationList
```

rationale: The change adds a check preventing a Safe contract from being added as its own owner unless it is an EIP‑7702 delegated account. Previously, self‑ownership could reduce the effective owner count, making the required signature threshold unreachable and potentially locking funds, which is a security‑relevant availability issue.

subject: Add EIP-7951 Signer Support (#1061)
body:
Fixes #1054

This PR adds support for EIP-7951 (and thus RIP-7212) signers to the
Safe contracts, allowing P-256 signers to also sign Safe transactions.
In particular, this is interesting as it allows things like secure
enclave signatures (as the Nist P-256 curve is supported there while the
secp256k1 curve it not).

The new signer works by adding a new signature type (arbitrarily chosen
to be 2), which checks that the `p256verify` precompile returns that a
signature is valid, and checks `address(keccak256(qx, qy))` is a Safe
owner (same address derivation scheme as EOAs, but for the secp256r1
curve).
rationale: The diff adds a new feature: signature type v==2 that verifies P-256 (secp256r1) signatures via the EIP-7951/RIP-7212 p256verify precompile, plus a new EIP7951 interface contract; the Certora harness/spec and test changes merely adapt existing checks (e.g., vA != 2) to the new signature type. No pre-existing incorrect or exploitable behaviour is corrected, so this is an enhancement rather than a bug or security fix.

subject: docs(FallbackManager): document CALL semantics, msg.sender rewrite, and security implications (#1106)
body:
Closes #532.

## What changed

### `contracts/interfaces/IFallbackManager.sol`
Expanded the `fallback()` NatSpec to document:
1. **Why `CALL` and not `DELEGATECALL`** — the handler executes in its
own storage context so it cannot read or write Safe state;
`DELEGATECALL` would give the handler unrestricted write access to all
Safe storage (contrast: modules already support `DELEGATECALL` when
owners explicitly enable it).
2. **`msg.sender` rewrite** — inside the handler's call frame
`msg.sender` is the Safe's own address, not the original external
caller.
3. **Security warning** — if the fallback handler exposes state-changing
functions that gate access on `msg.sender` alone (e.g. a token
contract), any external account can trigger those operations on the
Safe's behalf. Operators should only install purpose-built, audited
handlers.
4. **Caller recovery** — the original caller address is appended as the
last 20 bytes of calldata; handlers that inherit `HandlerContext` can
recover it via `_msgSender()`.

### `docs/overview.md`
Expanded the one-line "Fallback contract" entry with three sub-sections
that address both the original issue and the follow-up discussion in
#532:
- *How call forwarding works*
- *Why `CALL` instead of `DELEGATECALL`*
- *Security implications of `msg.sender` rewriting* (with a ⚠️ warning
block)

subject: Fix Revert Data Length in `CompatibilityFallbackHandler.simulate` (#1123)
body:
When the simulated call fails, `simulate` re-throws the error from
`response`, a `bytes` value laid out as `[length][data]`. The revert
started at the data (`add(response, 0x20)`) but used
`responseEncodedSize` (`length + 0x20`) as its size. So every re-thrown
error had 32 bytes of whatever memory followed `response` added to the
end.

This PR changes the revert size to `mload(response)`, so exactly
`length` bytes of revert data are returned.

The existing "should propagate revert message" test didn't catch this
because decoding `Error(string)` ignores trailing bytes. The new "should
propagate exact revert data" test compares the raw revert data byte for
byte.

This issue was submitted over the [bug bounty
program](https://docs.safefoundation.org/security/bug-bounty) but found
not to be in scope. Shout-out to the anonymous submitter who brought
this to our attention!

---

agree to the terms of the [Contributor License
Agreement](https://docs.safefoundation.org/cla).
rationale: The change corrects the revert size from using the encoded size (including a 32‑byte header) to the actual data length, fixing incorrect revert data propagation. No evidence in the diff shows exploitable impact; the commit notes the issue was out of scope for the bug bounty, indicating it is not considered a security vulnerability.

subject: Bind Approved Hash Signatures to dataHash When s Is Non-Zero (#1126)
body:
Fixed #187 

Approved hash signatures (`v = 1`) from the executor are not bound to
the hash being signed. If an owner submits the same `execTransaction`
call twice (for example, two identical transactions broadcast at the
same time), both calls succeed and execute for consecutive nonces,
because nothing ties the signature to a particular transaction hash.

This PR lets the `s` value of an approved hash signature optionally bind
it to a specific hash: when `s` is non-zero, `checkNSignatures` reverts
with `GS025` unless `s == dataHash`. Signatures with `s = 0` keep their
current behaviour, so existing signers are unaffected. The check applies
to all approved hash signatures, including hashes pre-approved via
`approveHash`, where it is redundant but harmless.

---

With the submission of this Pull Request, I confirm that I have read and
agree to the terms of the [Contributor License
Agreement](https://docs.safefoundation.org/cla).
rationale: The change adds a validation that approved hash signatures (v=1) with a non‑zero s must match the transaction data hash, preventing replay of the same execTransaction with different nonces. Previously signatures were not bound to the hash, allowing double execution and potential fund loss, which is a security defect.
